conclusion.justification: The report concludes that while older studies suggested a benefit, the best and most recent high-quality evidence (including updated Cochrane reviews and large RCTs) shows that probiotics likely do not shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea. Because it presents the claim as unsupported by rigorous current evidence while acknowledging older mixed findings, it leans towards rejecting the claim.

report:
## The Evidence Is Actually Mixed — "Yes" Is Overstated

Your assumption of a clear "yes" isn't well supported by the most rigorous recent evidence. The picture is more nuanced:

**Older meta-analyses suggested benefit.** Earlier Cochrane reviews (e.g., Allen 2010) and various smaller meta-analyses found probiotics, combined with oral rehydration, shortened diarrhea duration by roughly 25 hours and reduced stool frequency ([Cochrane 2010](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub3/abstract); [RACGP summary](https://www.racgp.org.au/clinical-resources/clinical-guidelines/handi/handi-interventions/nutrition/probiotics-for-acute-infectious-diarrhea)). These pooled many small, heterogeneous, often lower-quality trials.

**The updated 2020 Cochrane review reversed this conclusion.** After incorporating two large, rigorous, low-risk-of-bias multicenter trials, Cochrane now states: "Probiotics may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts. We do not know if they can shorten the time to recovery," with only low-to-moderate certainty evidence, and no clear effect on risk of diarrhea lasting ≥48 hours ([Cochrane 2020](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/)).

**Large, high-quality pediatric RCTs found no benefit.** Two major North American multicenter trials—NEJM 2018 (Freedman et al., combination Lactobacillus probiotic) and the PECARN LGG trial—found no significant improvement in diarrhea duration or severity in children with acute gastroenteritis presenting to emergency departments ([NEJM 2018](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597); [PECARN summary](https://pecarn.org/pecarn_news/probiotics-do-not-improve-the-outcomes-in-pediatric-acute-gastroenteritis/)).

**Bottom line:** Effects, if any, are likely small, strain-specific, and inconsistent across populations/settings. The best current evidence (large trials, updated Cochrane synthesis) does not confirm a clinically meaningful reduction in diarrhea duration for most patients, contradicting the simple "yes" answer suggested by older, smaller studies.
